claims.text: The early phase transition in solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is initiated by surface premelting.
Surface premelting begins preferentially in Cu-enriched regions.
Cu-enriched regions melt at lower temperatures than the remainder of the alloy.
Localized surface melting increases surface diffusion.
Increased surface diffusion accelerates compositional segregation.
Diffusion-enhanced segregation causes melting to propagate inward and culminate in a full phase transition.
The proposed starting nanoparticles are crystalline, fully solid, and relatively compositionally homogeneous.
Slight local Cu enrichment at the surface promotes surface diffusion and premelting.
Cu has a lower melting point than the other constituent elements.
Cu has lower cohesive energy than the other constituent elements.
Melting should initiate anisotropically at nanoparticle surfaces at temperatures below the overall melting point.
Early melting sites should spatially coincide with regions having higher Cu concentrations.
After surface melting begins, the melt front should progress rapidly into the nanoparticle core.
Conventional bulk melting would occur uniformly and at a higher temperature than the proposed localized surface onset.
The proposed mechanism should dominate when particles are sufficiently small for surface-to-volume effects to be important.
The proposed mechanism requires a heating rate slow enough to permit segregation.
Very rapid heating or differences in initial compositional homogeneity may obscure premelting behavior.
Nanoparticles with native Cu fluctuations should exhibit earlier and more localized surface melting than nanoparticles engineered to minimize surface Cu enrichment under the same heating profile.
